item.title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2zrn01pxko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial - Published President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress. Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection. Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access. Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday. He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party". Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia. They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries. The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives". It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region". "The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region," the state department added. Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November. The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history". The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin. This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets. However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron. This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external. Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m. Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018. Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered. The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen. The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces. The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said. Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published18 November 2025

item.title: Canadians dream of Europe as Carney floats longshot plan for living and working in EU
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx980qj57r89o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canadians dream of Europe as Carney floats longshot plan for living and working in EU - Published Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc. "I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto. Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy. "We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said. He also suggested Canada could join Erasmus+, the EU's multi-billion scholarship programme. Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture". But before Canadians start packing their bags - "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement. Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread. Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits. "It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said. Canadian social media has lit up with the topic. One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France. "Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter. The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US. Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool. "I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower. But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation. "I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said. Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US. "It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe." For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music. "I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added. "However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals." These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city. Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons. Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations. The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021. A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America. However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce. A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards. "It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday. Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations. And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble. "I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil. Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems." But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil. "I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid." item.title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
item.description:

========================================
This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern - Published The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention. This weekend more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers are battling it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton. "We've never had any media wanting to attend before," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC. But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes. While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans. And though influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern. "Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition. Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told the BBC he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue. "Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said. "I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on." The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane. But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language. "Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting. "It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right." Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks. But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing. Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion". And Ginn said: "If elite means having some expertise in the sport over 20 odd years, I'm proud of that." Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability. On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games. "Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said. There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide. The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered." In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics. The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle. But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors. The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week. So what about the crocodiles? They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't referenced in the media release about the technical assessment. That report itself has not yet been made public. The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times. "The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says. "Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free." Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile". Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added. The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped tens of millions of dollars into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy. "The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement. And those who argue the tabloid-friendly crocodile debate is overblown, say the biggest of the creatures live downstream. The less-dangerous freshwater crocodiles are more likely to be spotted in the rowing arena, they say. Also contested by government is the flood risk, though Rowing Queensland's O'Loughlin says that their schools event was due to be held on the Fitzroy in August 2024, but had to be moved after the course was washed away. Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue". The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders. For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water. Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games. "For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School. "The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally." 'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg. She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July. The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run. Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely. "This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo. In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act. The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas". Is Canada about to join the EU? Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union. Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member". The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member". The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means.
